newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels build administration in Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels build administration in Kisangani.

text.p: Rebels are building a local administration in Zaire's third largest city and say their five-month-old rebellion is turning into a popular uprising.
Rebel justice commissioner Mwanze Kongolo said late on Wednesday that rebel cadres would arrive in Kisangani on Thursday to explain to civic leaders the purpose of the rebellion and local elections.
Its seven communes would each elect a leader and they could nominate a candidate for mayor and a regional governor, he said.
"We are here to give them (residents) power denied to them for so long. That is the basic message we have and to illustrate it we will have visible -- but not perfect -- elections," he added.
Polls in other towns held by the rebels would also start within a week, said Kongolo, one of three rebel commissioners in Kisangani, the capital of the northeast.
The city, which fell last Saturday, is the greatest prize so far taken by the rebels in their five-month-old campaign to oust ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's ruler for 32 years.

The rebels say their armed rebellion is being transformed into a popular uprising since the fall of Kisangani as they tap into deep dissatisfaction with the government army and Mobutu's rule, which has virtually bankrupted the mineral-rich country.

"It was a tyrannical regime. There was no freedom of expression. The people resisted first in parliament, then with street protests and finally they have taken up arms," said Gilbert Kabasele, president of a rebel tribunal in Kisangani.
Boatmen on the Zaire River said government soldiers extorted up to 20 percent of their income from operating pirogues or canoes cut out of tree trunks across the broad waterway.
"Life is hard. We only do this job because there is no other work," said boatman Kombozi Pocho, adding they hid their canoes when troops fled last weekend to stop them being commandeered.

The rebels say they expect to meet little resistance in the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba, a centre of opposition to Mobutu's rule. Foreign mercenaries failed to save Kisangani, the hub of the army's failed counter-offensive in the east.
But a series of problems face the rebels as they seek to channel popular euphoria sweeping Kisangani after its fall.
They have to decide how to control the once-lucrative diamond industry, central to Kisangani's former prosperity as a commercial hub on the last navigable point on the Zaire River.
Boarded-up shops owned by diamond dealers line the streets of the city centre.

"People don't have to smuggle the gold and diamonds out of this country. They can stay here, pay low taxes and build good houses...just like in the gold rush in California," said Mawampanga Mwana Nanga, the rebels' finance commissioner.
In addition rebel leader Laurent Kabila has to hold together the rebel alliance in the face of growing business opportunities and he must control ethnic tensions which sparked the revolt.

The rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
The rebels say they are even replacing the name of Zaire, which was imposed by autocratic Mobutu, and renaming it Congo.
"This country of Congo can be the star of Africa. It can be a light to the rest of Africa. This is our vision," rebel political commissioner Deo Bugera told reporters in Kisangani.
